analysis.one_liner: Caps congressional campaign spending and donations, and bans party soft money in federal elections.
analysis.headline: The bill set a $1 million Senate and $200,000 House spending cap, but died in committee without a hearing, a vote, or a single cosponsor.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have rewritten the campaign finance rules for congressional elections. Senate candidates could spend at most $1 million per election cycle and House candidates at most $200,000; individual donations would be capped at $500. It would bar national and state party committees from spending anything on congressional races, cap local party help at $100, ban 'soft money' (unregulated money given to parties for supposedly non-candidate activity) on penalty of up to a year in prison, and require that donors live in the state or district where the election is held. It also imposed steep penalties: a winner who overspent the limit by more than 20 percent would forfeit the seat. The bill never got a committee hearing or a vote and expired when the 104th Congress ended.
analysis.who_benefits: Ordinary voters would benefit from lower-cost, more locally funded campaigns, since donors would have to live in the state or district and outside money from parties and PACs would be sharply restricted. Candidates without access to wealthy donors or national party money would face a lower spending ceiling on all sides, narrowing the money gap against well-funded opponents.

how_it_helps.text: Caps Senate campaign spending at $1,000,000 and House campaign spending at $200,000 per election cycle, limiting the amount of money needed to run for Congress.
Caps individual contributions at $500 per election and requires that donors reside in the state or district holding the election, reducing the influence of outside money.

Bars national and state party committees from making any expenditures in congressional elections and caps local party contributions at $100, while banning soft money and in-kind contributions with criminal penalties of up to one year in prison.

Imposes fines of 10 to 20 times any excess spending, and a candidate who wins while exceeding a limit by more than 20 percent must forfeit the office; a losing violator is barred from federal office for 10 years.

analysis.who_pays: National and state political parties would lose their ability to fund congressional campaigns, and large donors, out-of-state donors, and multicandidate PACs would see their giving capped or cut off. Wealthy self-funding candidates would be limited to $10,000 of their own money. Incumbents and challengers who currently rely on national party money and out-of-district contributions would have to run leaner campaigns.

drawbacks.text: Mandatory spending limits on candidates run into constitutional problems: the Supreme Court held in Buckley v. Valeo (1976) that limits on campaign spending by candidates and their committees violate the First Amendment, so this design would likely have been struck down in court unless it was structured as a voluntary system with benefits for compliance, as later reform bills were.

The contribution and spending ceilings were set at fixed dollar amounts with no adjustment mechanism, and critics of hard caps argue they can disadvantage challengers who need to raise name recognition quickly, potentially making seats safer for incumbents.
The bill did nothing about independent expenditures or spending by outside groups other than party committees, so money could have shifted to channels the bill did not address.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The goal — cutting the role of big money, party soft money, and out-of-district donors in congressional elections — is one most voters say they want, and the enforcement penalties were unusually serious. But the bill was written as a one-page set of hard caps with no voluntary-incentive structure, which the Supreme Court's campaign-spending rulings have made constitutionally doubtful, and it left independent and outside-group spending untouched. A serious version of this reform would need a different legal design, which is a reason the bill's substance was weaker than its intent.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and sent to the House Oversight Committee on the day it was filed, and the committee never took it up, so it died when the 104th Congress ended in January 1997.

narrative.text: Rep. Harold Volkmer, a Missouri Democrat, introduced the Campaign Spending Limitation Reform Act of 1996 on June 13, 1996, with no cosponsors.
The bill was referred the same day to the House Committee on House Oversight, the committee with jurisdiction over campaign finance.
The committee took no further action on the bill — no hearing, no markup, no committee vote — and it never reached the House floor.
The 104th Congress ended on January 3, 1997, and the bill expired without a vote in either chamber.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: The existing campaign finance system stayed intact: national and state party committees, large out-of-state donors, and PACs kept spending on congressional races without the caps or the soft money ban, and incumbent officeholders continued to raise money under the looser rules.

sides.party_line_note: The bill had a single Democratic sponsor, no cosponsors of either party, and never reached a vote, so no partisan breakdown of support or opposition exists in the record.

industries.industry: National and state political party committees
industries.note: The bill would have prohibited national and state party committees from spending anything on Senate and House elections, cutting off a major funding channel for congressional campaigns. Party committees relied on that spending power to shape elections, so their interest ran against the bill's restrictions.

PAC contributions to congressional candidates would be capped at $2,500, and PACs without members in the relevant state or district would be barred entirely. PAC money is a core funding source for congressional campaigns, so the caps would have shrunk their role.
Individual contributions would be capped at $500 per cycle and restricted to people living in the state or district where the election is held, cutting off big-ticket and outside-money fundraising.
